messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 47
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Plumber
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 62

She arrives for our session still wearing her work boots, the soles stained with dried mud and copper dust. She apologizes for the smell—says she came straight from a job replacing a water heater in a basement. She sits on the edge of the chair, hands clasped between her knees, eyes scanning the room once before settling on the floor. She tells me she doesn’t like basements. Never has.

As a plumber, she spends most of her days in them. She took the job twelve years ago, right after her second child was born, because she needed something steady and she was good with her hands. Her father had taught her how to fix a leaky pipe when she was twelve—one of the rare moments he wasn’t angry. She laughs dryly when she says this, then stops. The laugh dies in her throat.

The abuse started long before the pipe lesson. She was five, maybe six, when her mother first locked her in the closet. Her mother was a devout woman, strict, quick to punish. The beatings came with a leather belt, a wooden spoon, sometimes the heel of a shoe. The worst part, she says, was not the pain. It was the waiting. The sound of footsteps on the stairs. The creak of the door. The certain knowledge that she had done something wrong, even if she didn’t know what.

She learned to read her mother’s moods by the tightness of her jaw, the way she set down a cup. She learned to walk quietly, to make herself small, to never ask for anything. She still walks quietly. Her husband teases her about it, says she creeps up on him. She doesn’t tell him it’s survival.

At work, she is known as dependable, meticulous, a little distant. She prefers jobs where she works alone. When a customer stands too close while she’s under the sink, her shoulders lock up. Her heart starts pounding. She has to count the threads on a pipe fitting—one, two, three, four—to stop herself from crawling out and running. She keeps her tools organized in the same order every day. If something is misplaced, she feels a sharp spike of panic, like she’s forgotten a rule and punishment is coming.

She has been married for twenty-two years. Her husband is gentle, patient. He doesn’t raise his voice. But sometimes, when he speaks to her from another room, she flinches. She hates herself for it. She has two children in college now. When they were small, she never spanked them. She would walk away instead, stand in the bathroom with the water running until her hands stopped shaking.

Nighttime is the hardest. She lies awake, replaying scenes she has never told anyone. The feel of the closet door clicking shut. The sting across her thighs. The silence after the beating, when her mother would pray aloud, asking God to forgive her for having such a difficult child. She still believes, somewhere deep, that she was a bad child. That she is still a difficult person to love.

She doesn’t cry in session. She holds herself very still. She tells me she came because her husband said she seemed “not really here” some days, and because she found herself screaming at a broken pipe last week, crying and hitting it with a wrench until her knuckles bled. She didn’t feel the pain until later. She just felt the rage, old and hot, rising from a place she thought she had sealed shut.

When the hour ends, she stands, zips her jacket, and says she has another job in the afternoon—a clogged drain in a crawl space. She will have to lie on her stomach in the dark for hours. She will do it because she knows how. Because the dark, at least, is familiar.
